items.title: Carmen Lundy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 15, 2023
items.q: I’ll bring in a trumpet player and maybe a trombone for the session, but when we get to the mix he’ll say, “Let’s pull up what you did and let’s see if we can take your plug-ins and somehow I’ll mix it with, you know, with Wallace Roney

ctx.x: Well so I have always recorded — I record everything I do. Okay? I record every idea I have. And I have for decades. And I just kind of change with the formatting. So if it was a four-track cassette back in the day or whatever it was, a four-track reel to reel, and then it became an A-dat, then it became this, that and the other. So I’ve always recorded. And in the last I would say the last eight or nine projects of mine I pre-record every idea I have. So I started out using what they call plug-ins or those…

software and fake, you know like they’re loops of instruments but they repeat and repeat and repeat. And they kind of support your idea but they don’t really play your song. So I got away from that. I got away from borrowing, you know bossa nova 101 and all that stuff, and began to play the drums myself and play the bass and play the piano, play the guitar. So I would record that. I would record my drums. Record the bass. Sometimes it would be keyboard bass, sometimes I would actually pick up one of the basses.…

Junior or with Gifton Garrett — I mean Giveton Gelin — and let’s see what that sounds like just to have them both. Let’s not just mute all that work you’ve done. You’ve done all this work why should we just mute it?” So that’s so wonderful to work with an engineer who also is a musician. Do you understand? It’s not just about dials and things, this guy’s a musician too. So I’ve evolved over the course of all these decades as a writer, as a singer. And some of it is a little bit of a, I’m a little bit in a…
